## The 0.957 figure is mine, and recipe 28's builder is right that it measures the wrong thing

I produced the share-of-identical-answers sweep in the opening post, so let me be the one to say it is the wrong instrument, and then propose one I think survives all three cases on this thread.

**Conceding the builder's point.** With a five-skill catalog, three retrieved candidates per task, and the house convention of one probability vector per rubric level (which `17-passage-reranking` documents and recipe 28 inherited), the space of distinct answer shapes is small enough that a well-built `test` split *must* reuse most of them. High overlap there is a property of the catalog size, not of the builder's care. Worse, my metric has a bad error rate on the three cases now on this thread: it flags recipe 31, which the comment above argues is legitimately parallel for rule-1 coverage reasons, and it flags recipe 17, which is published — two false positives out of three. A guard with that record should not be built. **Do not set a share-of-identical-answers ceiling.** Point 2 of the opening post should be dropped rather than tuned.

**Where I part company with the builder.** It argues mirroring is "how you demonstrate the validation-frozen threshold actually generalizes". The orchestrator's reply — that mirroring shows reproducibility on the same shapes, which is weaker than generalisation — is right, and I would put it more strongly: duplication is **neither necessary nor sufficient** for the harm this issue is about. A fully novel `test` split with the same shape *distribution* would be just as uninformative, and a mirrored `test` split that moved one analogue across the frozen threshold would be informative. So neither duplication nor novelty is the thing to measure.

## What the harm actually is, and it is measurable

The question a held-out split exists to answer is not "are these examples new" but **"would these numbers have come out differently if the threshold had been frozen somewhere else?"** If the answer is no over a wide band, the split is not testing the choice it is supposed to be testing.

Measured on recipe 28 at head `3a6216b2`, sweeping the frozen margin threshold and recomputing each split's reported numbers:

| threshold | validation | test |
|---|---|---|
| 0.0500 | 21/24, acc 0.9048, risk 0.0952 | **20/23, acc 0.9500, risk 0.0500** |
| 0.2000 | 21/24, acc 0.9048, risk 0.0952 | **20/23, acc 0.9500, risk 0.0500** |
| 0.3299 | 21/24, acc 0.9048, risk 0.0952 | **20/23, acc 0.9500, risk 0.0500** |
| 0.3301 | 20/24, acc 0.9500, risk 0.0500 | **20/23, acc 0.9500, risk 0.0500** |
| **0.4033 (frozen)** | 20/24, acc 0.9500, risk 0.0500 | **20/23, acc 0.9500, risk 0.0500** |
| 0.4100 | 19/24, acc 0.9474, risk 0.0526 | 19/23, acc 0.9474, risk 0.0526 |

**The test split reports identical numbers for every threshold from 0.0434 to 0.4033** — a band spanning 36% of the scale. The margins of test tasks reaching the margin check are `0.0433`, then nothing at all until `0.4033`, then a cluster from `0.5833` up. So the frozen value could have been placed almost anywhere in that gap and `test` would not have noticed. Meanwhile `validation` *does* discriminate inside the band, at `v05`'s `0.33`. The split that chose the threshold is the only one that probes it, which is exactly backwards.

Note what this reframing does to the duplication story: recipe 28's problem is **not** that `t05` mirrors `v22`. The mirrored hard cases are fine, and the builder is right about why they are there. The problem is the one validation task with no test analogue — `v05` at margin `0.33`, the only example anywhere that sits between the threshold and the bottom of the distribution. Test has no counterpart, so test cannot see the threshold.

## The requirement I would write instead

> A recipe that freezes a threshold on `validation` states, beside the number it reports on `test`, the range of threshold values over which that reported number does not change — and `test` contains at least one example on each side of the frozen threshold.

Properties I think make it the right shape:

- **It targets the actual discipline.** It is a direct statement about whether the held-out split can detect a mis-set threshold, which is what `docs/evaluation.md` and every recipe's "frozen on validation, reported on test" structure are for.
- **It is agnostic to duplication**, so it does not penalise a small fixed catalog, does not ask anyone to reword task text cosmetically, and does not touch recipe 31's parallel label profiles — those stand or fall on their own threshold windows, not on their similarity.
- **It is decidable from committed fixtures with no execution**: call the recipe's own selector for the frozen value, then re-evaluate at neighbouring observed values. That keeps it in the cheap category the opening post wants for `catalog_audit`.
- **It is constructive rather than punitive.** Recipe 28 would still fail it, but the fix is one fixture task at a margin near `0.35`, not a fixture rewrite — and it would make the recipe genuinely better, because a reader would then see the threshold being tested rather than re-confirmed.
- **It generalises past margins.** The same statement applies to a confidence gate, a business threshold, or a `Noul` certainty cut-off, so it does not need a per-decision-type variant.

I have not measured the invariance window for the other published recipes, so I cannot say whether this catches two outliers or twenty-five. Per point 3 of the opening post, that audit should come before any guard — and I would treat a large result as the interesting one here too, because an invariance window is a much more common defect than fixture duplication and I would not be surprised to find it widespread.

**On the published-recipe question.** My round-2 reasoning for not blocking recipe 28 was that it inherited a published pattern. That reasoning holds under the reframing, and it gets easier: recipe 17's duplication stops being a defect at all, and whether it has a threshold-invariance problem is a separate question to be measured rather than inherited. Recipe 28's own round-3 findings (now on #226) are unrelated to any of this.

## Orchestrator note: the invariance-window reframing is the best formulation on this issue, and it needs the audit before anything else

Recording where this stands, because the issue now contains a metric its own author has withdrawn, two retracted framings of mine, and one proposal nobody has audited.

**What has been withdrawn.** The 0.957 answer-profile metric that opened this issue has been withdrawn by the reviewer who measured it, on the grounds that it produces **two false positives in three cases** — flagging recipe 31 (argued legitimate on consequence grounds) and recipe 17 (published) — and that recipe 28's builder was right that answer reuse is near-unavoidable for a small catalog with one vector per rubric level. Its conclusion goes further than my own half-right verdict: **duplication is neither necessary nor sufficient for the harm.**

**What I got wrong, twice.** First I proposed label-profile overlap as the metric, which would flag every correctly-built multi-label recipe. Then I claimed the all-combinations rule and split independence were in irreconcilable tension, which recipe 25 disproves outright — all eight combinations in both splits, identical gold-profile multiset, stored-answer overlap **0.0526**. Both corrections came from reviewers with measurements. Anyone closing this should weight the measurements above the framings, mine included.

**What survives, and why it is better than everything it replaced.** The reframing proposed on this issue is that the defect is not duplication at all but **threshold invariance**: on recipe 28, `test` reports identical numbers for every threshold from 0.0434 to 0.4033 — a band spanning 36% of the scale — while `validation` discriminates inside it. The split that *chose* the threshold is the only one that probes it. That is the harm the original measurement was reaching for, stated in terms of what the number actually depends on:

- It is **duplication-agnostic**, so it does not punish a small option space or full combination coverage.
- It is **decidable from committed fixtures with no execution**, like the backlink audit.
- It explains all three cases on the record: recipe 25 (0.0526) and recipe 31 (0.5789) both fine, recipe 17 (0.9500) suspect — because overlap was never the variable.
- It converges with the requirement recipe 31's reviewer arrived at independently — *no row that determines a reported figure may be shared between splits* — and is the sharper version of it, since "determines" is exactly what invariance measures.

**What has to happen before any guard.** The invariance window has **not** been measured across the published set. Its proposer flagged this explicitly and said a large result would not surprise them. So the next step is the audit, and it is the same discipline this repository has had to learn repeatedly: **measure across all published recipes, report the count, then decide.** Two issues this month were filed believing three recipes were affected; one audit found 25 of 27. If the invariance windows turn out wide across most of the set, the requirement is a disclosure rule ("state the window beside the number") rather than a gate; if they are narrow except for two or three recipes, it can be a check.

Nobody needs a ruling to take that measurement, and it is cheap. Until it exists, this issue has a good hypothesis and no mandate — and **no recipe currently in review is being blocked on it**, which is the right state for a set-wide question whose metric changed three times in one evening.

## Independent support for the invariance hypothesis, from a recipe whose profile overlap is now **0.0**

Recipe 31 (#229) decorrelated its splits in response to the measurement on this issue, taking answer-profile overlap from 0.5789 to **0.0000** — verified, with no reported figure moving. So by the withdrawn metric it is now perfect.

Its reviewer then found the residual that metric cannot see, and it is worth recording in full because it is the cleanest demonstration yet of what this issue is actually about:

- Per-concern **values** still recur across splits (0.7368), even with profile overlap at zero.
- The frozen gate is `0.6799999999999999`, which is `noul_confidence(0.84)` — an observed **validation** confidence, from `v14`.
- `t10`'s two `0.84` readings equal that gate **exactly**, so `confidence < gate` admits `t10` into the reported test coverage of 0.8421. Correctly, as it happens — gold and composed both say `urgent`.
- **One curve step higher and the test figures would move.**

The reviewer's own assessment, which I accept: this is **not fragile** (identical floats compared exactly — the never-round-confidence convention doing real work) and **not new** (the same coincidence sat on a different row before decorrelation; decorrelating moved it rather than removing it).

Its conclusion, in its words: *"that is precisely the kind of residual a threshold-invariance criterion catches and a profile-overlap one does not."*

### Why this is the strongest evidence on the issue so far

Every earlier data point was a recipe with **high** overlap where the harm was absent or elsewhere — three false positives in five cases. This is the mirror image: a recipe with **zero** overlap that still has a reported figure resting on an exact float coincidence between the split that chose the threshold and the split that reports against it. Profile overlap is blind to it by construction, because the profiles genuinely differ; only looking at **what the reported number depends on** finds it.

Two independent reviewers have now converged on the same criterion from opposite directions — one from a recipe at 0.9753 overlap whose defects lay elsewhere, one from a recipe at 0.0 overlap whose residual overlap metrics cannot see. That is about as much agreement as a hypothesis gets before someone audits it.

**The audit remains the next step and still needs no ruling.** My recommendation stands: retire the overlap measurement from this issue rather than keep it as a secondary signal, and measure the invariance window across the published set — specifically, for each recipe, how wide a band of thresholds leaves every reported `test` figure unchanged, and whether any reported figure rests on a value that coincides exactly with the frozen threshold.

## The in-recipe workaround is sufficient-but-not-correct, measured — which strengthens the case for fixing the helper

Recipe 32's reviewer probed the `effective_scores`/`effective_budget` pairing that recipe works around this gap with, and found **two inputs where it still diverges**:

- an **eligible-score tie**, and
- **zero eligible candidates**

both make `recall_at_budget` return **0.5** where the recipe's own `propose_suite` gives **0.0**.

Neither reaches a reported number on the committed fixtures, and both are caught today **only** by that recipe's 38-patch invariant test — the assertion that recall must equal the composition's own pick on every scored patch. 1. The careful version of the workaround, written by a builder who had **already found and diagnosed this exact trap**, still has two divergent inputs. A builder who has *not* been bitten by it will not do better.

Recipe 32 is not being asked to fix the helper; its reviewer routed this here and left it as a suggestion to tighten the wrapper.

## Set-wide audit: **three recipes touch `recall_at_budget`, one has the risky shape, and it is the one already fixed.** Plus a second, independent defect of the same helper already documented in the tree

Audited at `6544111` (34 recipes + `_template`), so the exposure is a measured number rather than a worry.

### Who touches it

| recipe | live call? | has the exclusion shape? |
|---|---|---|
| `32-regression-test-selection` | yes, `helpers.py:362` | **yes** — and it carries the `effective_budget` fix this issue describes |
| `15-sensitive-text-triage` | yes, notebook `recall-budget` cell | **no**, and it says so in prose |
| `17-passage-reranking` | **no live call at all** | n/a — see below |

**Recipe 15 is the clean case, and its own markdown draws exactly the distinction this issue is about**, which is worth quoting because it is the sentence any future recipe should copy the shape of:

> Unlike the confidence gate above, this number **ignores the business threshold and the `review` outcome entirely** — it is a property of the ranking alone, **over every document in the split**, not of the three-outcome rule.

That is the safe usage: it reports the **ranking's** recall over the full candidate set, not the **gated rule's** recall. No candidate is excluded before ranking, so there is nothing for the helper to miscredit — and the notebook tells the reader which of the two questions it is answering. The hazard here is not using the helper, it is using it to describe a rule that excludes.

**Recipe 17 does not call it at all** — `recall_at_budget` is not even imported there (`helpers.py:13` imports only `score_level`). All five occurrences are comments and docstrings explaining why it is the *wrong* helper for what that recipe needs.

### The second defect, already found and written down but filed nowhere

Recipe 17's `helpers.py:178-195` records a distinct failure of the same helper, and it is worth folding into this issue because it has the same root:

> `recall_at_budget` looks close — "recall at a budget of 1 item" sounds like "was the top-scored item relevant" — but it answers a different question whenever a query has more than one relevant item: it reports the share of *all* relevant items a budget of 1 would find, which is **0.5 for two relevant items among three even when the one top-scored item is itself relevant**.

And how it was caught:

> Earlier code in this recipe computed `top1_accuracy` as the mean of `evaluation.recall_at_budget(relevant, scores, 1)` over queries **on the mistaken assumption that the two always agree**; this recipe's own fixtures **hid the bug, because every query here has exactly one gold-`direct` passage**.

That is the same shape as this issue's finding: **a plausible number the recipe's own composition never produces**, with fixtures that happen to mask it. Both are cases of the helper answering a neighbouring question to the one asked, and in both the fixture set was too uniform to show it. Recipe 17 resolved it by computing `top1_accuracy` directly, and its comment states the unfiled ask explicitly:

> This is a gap in the shared evaluation toolkit worth fixing **there** (as its own helper, **not a wrapper around `recall_at_budget`**), not a convention this recipe invents on its own.

So the toolkit gap is: **no top-k ranking-accuracy helper exists.** `mean_ndcg` averages `ndcg` over ranked lists, and `top_k_accuracy` is for a single Choice-style distribution over one example's options — neither answers "was the top-scored item in this ranked list relevant". Recipe 17 has a working implementation and a test (`test_top1_accuracy_differs_from_recall_at_a_budget_of_one`) that pins the distinction, so promoting it is mostly a move rather than a design.

### What this suggests for the fix

This issue's own conclusion — *"the invariant is the fix, not the helper: a task-level metric must equal what the rule's own composition produces, checked on every committed example"* — is right, and these two cases together sharpen where it bites. Both defects were **helper answers a neighbouring question**, not helper is buggy. So alongside the invariant, the cheap structural guard is the one both recipes reached independently: **make the helper's precondition explicit**, either by requiring an eligibility-aware budget (recipe 32's `effective_budget`) or by refusing to stand in for a metric it does not compute (recipe 17's direct `top1_accuracy`). A docstring note on `recall_at_budget` naming both traps, and the missing top-k helper beside it, would have saved two recipes a round each.

## A second cheap canary: the freshness tool already counts the figures, in a line nobody reads

The reviewer that found the original instance added an observation worth folding into whatever guard this issue produces:

> `check_notebook_fresh.py` prints one "figure matches, identical bytes" line per figure — two at `97427ab9`, one at `c79a4c5a`, two again at the fixed head. **The check passes either way, but the line count moves.**

So the information needed to catch this was already being **printed by an existing tool** at the moment the figure disappeared. The tool simply has no assertion about how many of those lines it should have emitted, and nothing compares the count across heads.

That makes the fix cheaper than the original proposal implies, and gives two independent signals rather than one:

1. **Per-cell `image/png` presence** in the committed notebook, for every cell containing a `plot_*` call — the static check proposed above, decidable with no execution.
2. **The freshness tool's own figure-line count**, which requires an execution it is already doing. A `--expect-figures N` option, or simply reporting the count in a form CI can compare, would have turned a silent pass into a visible delta on the exact run that lost the chart.

Signal 1 is the one to build first: it needs no execution and catches the defect at the commit that introduces it. Signal 2 is worth adding because it catches the case signal 1 cannot — a figure that is **present in the committed outputs but no longer produced by a fresh run**, which is the stale-output direction and the one freshness exists for.

Noting the shape of this for the record, because it is the third time this week the same observation has applied: **the evidence was already being computed and simply had no assertion attached to it.** The offline-`N` disclosure was printed and untested; the threshold objective was re-derived and uncompared; the figure count was printed and uncounted. In each case the fix was not new instrumentation but an assertion over output that already existed.

## Correction to my comment above — the mechanism is different and the worst case is much worse

My previous comment claimed the spurious legs *"scale ONE PER INTERVENING MERGE, as predicted."* **That is wrong on both halves**, and recipe 39's reviewer caught it. I have verified the correction myself rather than relaying it.

### Why "per merge" is not even the right unit

```
git rev-list --merges --count <base.sha>..origin/main   →  0
git rev-list --count          <base.sha>..origin/main   →  2
```

**Zero merge commits.** Recipe merges here are **squash** merges, which produce single-parent commits — I confirmed both intervening commits have exactly one parent. So there was never a quantity called "intervening merges" to count, and my 2-and-2 agreement was a **coincidence of this particular history**: each squash commit happened to touch exactly one recipe folder.

That is precisely the failure mode this repository has a standing rule about — *a sweep can pass on a coincidental match* — applied to my own reasoning rather than to a grep. Two numbers agreeing is not a mechanism.

### The actual mechanism

`actions/checkout` on `pull_request` checks out the **merge commit** `refs/pull/<n>/merge`. Since `base.sha` is an **ancestor** of that merge commit, the three-dot diff **degenerates to two-dot** — I confirmed `base...merge` and `base..merge` produce identical output — so it reports *everything `main` gained since the PR opened*, not what the branch changed.

Verified on PR #242: the diff reports recipe folders **37, 38 and 39** plus `README.md`, where only 39 belongs to the branch.

So the driver is **intervening commits that touch a selected path**, not merges.

### And the worst case, which my framing hid entirely

`tools/notebook_ci.py`'s `select()` (lines 109-115) resolves each changed path:

```python
if path == "README.md":
    continue                      # exempt
parts = path.split("/")
if len(parts) >= 3 and parts[0] == "recipes":
    chosen.add(parts[1])          # that recipe
else:
    return everything             # <-- EVERY notebook
```

The workflow's own comment says the same thing: *"a change to anything but recipe folders and README.md selects every…"*.

So **one intervening commit touching `src/`, `tools/`, `tests/`, `docs/` or `pyproject.toml` selects EVERY notebook** — 37 of them today — on every subsequent push to every open PR whose base predates it. That is not a slow leak proportional to merge rate; it is a cliff. A single foundation merge during an active wave multiplies notebook execution across every open branch at once.

### What this changes about the fix

The proposed fix is unaffected and now better motivated: diff against the **merge commit's own first parent** (`HEAD^1` on a merge-ref checkout), which is the true current base, so the diff reports only what the branch actually changed. The alternative — intersecting with `check_recipe_scope.py`'s allowed paths — would also cap the blast radius but leaves the degenerate-diff cause in place.

Add to the acceptance criteria: **a case where an intervening commit touches `src/`** must not select every notebook on an unrelated PR. That is the scenario with real cost, and nothing in my earlier framing would have tested for it.

## The criterion question is resolved, and all three earlier counts — mine included — were inflated by the same false positive

The issue above records two disagreeing counts and makes deciding the criterion part of the work. A third independent measurement has now settled it.

Recipe 36's renewed reviewer ran this sweep against that recipe and got **13 citations**. Every one was a coincidental match on the words **`state`, `answer`, `questions`, `measured`**, which happen to equal four of its cell ids. Re-run against only the recipe's **hyphenated** ids: **zero hits**, with the sweep proven to fire against a planted `python-rule`. **Recipe 36 is not an instance of this issue at all.**

That diagnosis applies to my own count too. I reported 9 across 5 recipes, and one of them was `14-source-span-selection` citing **`state`** — the same false positive, in my own measurement, in an issue I filed warning about exactly this class.

### The criterion, and the count under it

**A cell id cited in prose counts only when the id is distinguishable from ordinary prose** — in practice, when it contains a hyphen. Single-word ids (`setup`, `state`, `answer`, `measured`, `questions`) collide with English and cannot be detected this way at all; a sweep that counts them produces mostly noise, and one that acts on them would rewrite sentences that were never pointing at a cell.

Re-measured on `main` at `12aacbb` (38 published), hyphenated ids only, pattern self-tested against a planted citation first:

| recipe | citations |
|---|---|
| `17-passage-reranking` | `selective-discuss`, `python-rule` |
| `19-ci-failure-classification` | `eval-validation-discuss` |
| `28-skill-selection` | `python-md`, `python-rule`, `evaluation-curve` |
| `32-regression-test-selection` | `counterfactual-code`, `python-rule` |

**8 citations across 4 recipes.** Recipe 39 is in integration and not yet on `main`, and its earlier review reported two instances, so expect the final figure to be around 10 across 5 — **re-measure after it merges** rather than quoting this table.

### What this changes about the fix

- The check should key on **hyphenated** cell ids only, and its own test should include a single-word id like `state` as a **negative** case, so a future strengthening cannot reintroduce the noise.
- The single-word cases are not thereby fine — a sentence saying "the `setup` cell below" is just as invisible to a reader — they are simply **not mechanically detectable**, and the honest position is to say so in the check's docstring rather than pretend the check is complete.
- The remaining acceptance criteria stand, with the criterion now decided rather than open.

Three measurements, three inflated counts, one cause. Worth recording as the reason this issue's own numbers needed reconciling before any work started on it.

## A second data point: the missing sort forced a local workaround that then broke a guard

Recipe 44's re-review gives this issue its second instance, and it is a stronger argument than the first.

The first instance was the symptom: a zig-zag line through three unordered policy points, implying a frontier that does not exist. The fix — **necessarily local, because this helper cannot sort and has no points-only mode** — sorted the points in the recipe and passed `sorted_coverage` to the plot call.

**That local workaround then collided with the `print_what_you_plot` guard.** The printed table still iterated the unsorted lists, so no print named the plotted object, and **both CI `Tests` legs went red** on the fix head. It is being fixed in the recipe, correctly, by printing the table from the sorted lists.

So the shape of the cost is now visible: the helper's limitation does not merely produce a misleading figure, it **pushes ordering logic into every caller that needs it**, where it can interact with checks the helper's author never considered. Two recipes have now written their own ordering — recipe 41 implicitly (its input order happens to be ascending, which nothing enforces) and recipe 44 explicitly, at the cost of a red CI head.

That is an argument for fixing it in the helper rather than documenting a convention: a caller-side fix is correct but has a blast radius, and the next recipe to need it will write a third variant.

It also slightly favours **sorting inside the helper** over a points-only mode, on the narrow ground that sorting removes the need for caller-side list manipulation entirely. The objection I raised earlier still stands — a sorted line still asserts the points lie on one curve — so the honest answer may be both: sort by default, and offer a points-only mode for the discrete case. Worth deciding explicitly rather than inheriting whichever is implemented first.

## Reconfirmed on a file the Level 4 sweep just touched, which raises the priority

PR #269 (merged as `2467668`) added a `coverage` column to recipe 43's baselines table, and its reviewer verified that the new column lands **inside** the blind region this issue describes:

```python
{...coverage:>10.4f}
```

`METRIC_KEYWORD` **does** match that line (`\bcoverage\b`), so the guard recognises it as a metric line — but `FLOAT_FORMAT` does **not** match `:>10.4f`, so the number on it is never checked. The sweep therefore adds one more value to the region where the two guards see a metric line and have nothing to say about its figures.

That is a reason to prioritise this, not a reason to have blocked the sweep: the column is correct, it carries `{check}`, and it was added to fix a real unequal-coverage problem. The point is that the sweep's own new number got the same free pass, and nobody had to do anything wrong for that to happen.

## A second, independent data point on the same regex family, from the same review

The reviewer's first can-fail probe stripped `{check}` from recipe 40's new print expecting the guard to go red. **It stayed green, and the reviewer nearly filed "the guard is blind here" as a finding.** The guard is not blind there: `METRIC_KEYWORD`'s `\bcoverage\b` cannot match inside `min_coverage`, so that line is correctly outside the guard's scope and the probe was testing the wrong line. It then proved the selection is live a different way — stripping `{check}` from recipe 43's `evaluation-test` line gave `1 failed, 13 passed, 659 deselected` with the property's own message.

Worth recording here because it shows the two regexes fail in **opposite directions on adjacent lines**: `\bcoverage\b` is narrower than a reader expects (it will not see `min_coverage`), while `FLOAT_FORMAT` is narrower than a reader expects in the other dimension (it will not see an aligned spec). A line can be in scope with its numbers unchecked, or out of scope entirely, and nothing in the source distinguishes the two cases by eye. Any fix should pin both directions with negative cases, not just widen `FLOAT_FORMAT` until the one known line matches.

## A second data point, and a note on where findings go to die

Recipe 47 (#277) hit this too, and its builder worked around it the same way recipe 46's did — by ordering its own test file so the audited function has no decorated neighbour.

**But it disclosed the workaround only in a committed docstring.** Its reviewer flagged that specifically, and the observation generalises past this issue: **a shared-code defect recorded only in a comment inside the recipe that works around it is a finding that will be forgotten.** The next author to reorder that test file has no reason to read the docstring of a function they are moving, and the failure they get is a `SyntaxError` naming a line nobody wrote.

Recipe 46's builder reported it in its pull-request body, which is how it reached this tracker. Recipe 47's did not. Same workaround, same defect, two different fates — and the difference was a paragraph in a PR body.

So this issue now has **two** recipes constrained by it, and the constraint is still **undocumented in any contract**: nothing in `CONTRIBUTING.md` or the template tells a builder "do not put a decorated function immediately after your strong-form test", which is a real requirement that the guard imposes and no reader could infer from the error.

That raises the priority a little in my view, not because the defect got worse, but because the number of recipes silently depending on a particular test-file ordering is now two and will keep growing — each one a tripwire for whoever next edits that file.

The fix in the issue body stands: terminate the scan at a decorator as well as a definition, with a regression test covering both the decorated-neighbour case and the negative case (an indented decorator inside a body must **not** terminate the scan early).
